content: Adjustment disorder is characterized by an emotional and behavioral response that arises within three months of a stressful life event. This response is more intense or severe than what would typically be expected for the nature of the event. Symptoms of Adjustment Disorder: For a diagnosis of adjustment disorder, the symptoms must be significant enough to interfere with the individual’s work or social life. Common symptoms include: Agitation Behavioral disturbances Depressed mood Palpitations Physical complaints Trembling or twitching Symptoms generally begin within three months of the stressor and typically resolve within six months unless the stressor persists (e.g., chronic illness or living in a dangerous environment). In some cases, symptoms can become severe, leading to suicidal thoughts or suicide attempts. Causes of Adjustment Disorder: In adults, adjustment disorder often arises from marital or financial difficulties. In adolescents, common stressors include: Family conflicts School-related problems Issues related to sexuality Other stressors that can affect individuals of any age include: The death of a loved one Major life changes Unexpected catastrophes It is not possible to predict which individuals exposed to the same stressor will develop adjustment disorder. Factors such as financial stability, social support, career opportunities, and recreational activities can influence how well a person copes with stress. Additionally, susceptibility to stress may be affected by: Coping strategies Intelligence Flexibility Genetic predisposition Social skills When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: You should contact a healthcare provider if you develop symptoms of adjustment disorder. Diagnosis: To diagnose adjustment disorder, the following criteria must be met: Symptoms must clearly follow a stressor. Symptoms must be more severe than what would typically be expected. There should be no evidence of other underlying disorders. Symptoms should not be part of normal grieving for the death of a loved one. Treatment Options: The primary goal of treatment is to alleviate symptoms and help the individual return to their previous level of functioning before the stressful event occurred. Individual therapy can assist the person in: Receiving support Identifying abnormal responses to the stressor Maximizing the use of their strengths Mental health professionals often recommend some form of talk therapy to help individuals identify or learn alternative responses to stressors in their lives. Types of therapy may include: Behavioral therapy Individual psychotherapy Family therapy Self-help groups Medications may be used in conjunction with other treatments, depending on the symptoms. These may include: Anti-anxiety medications Antidepressants Antipsychotic medications (rarely) Stimulants (for patients who are severely withdrawn) Where to Find Medical Care: Hospitals and clinics specializing in mental health can provide treatment for adjustment disorder. Prognosis: Adjustment disorders typically resolve quickly, often without any lasting symptoms. Prevention: There is no known way to prevent adjustment disorder. However, strong support from friends and family can be beneficial in coping with stress.
